extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, patent attorneys, and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting claim language during patent examination, including treatment of preambles, transitional phrases, contingent clauses, printed matter, machine‑readable media, and inherency in prior art. Provides standards, examples, and case law to decide whether particular claim language is limiting and how to apply rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101/102/103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble as claim limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether preamble recitations are structural limitations or mere statements of purpose/use depends on review of the entire record and what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass; if the claim body fully and intrinsically sets forth all limitations, a preamble stating purpose/intended use is not a limitation, except where the preamble provides context or is relied on during prosecution to distinguish prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve by looking to the claim body, specification, and prosecution history. Examples/case law: Corning Glass Works (review entirety), Pitney Bowes v. Hewlett‑Packard (preamble stating purpose not limiting), Rowe v. Dror, Kropa v. Robie, STX LLC v. Brine. If preamble language forms the basis for distinguishing prior art in prosecution (clear reliance), it becomes a claim limitation (Metabolite Labs.; Catalina Mktg. Intl.). Also can be a limitation where preamble discloses a fundamental characteristic of the invention (Poly‑America). For method claims directed to treating people, preamble meaning (e.g., “a human in need thereof”) may be limiting (Jansen, Nantkwest, Cruciferous Sprout Litig.). During examination, evaluate whether recited purpose results in a structural (or manipulative) difference over the prior art; if so, it limits the claim (In re Otto; In re Sinex; In re Schreiber).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase: 'comprising' (open/including)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional term 'comprising' (synonymous with including/containing/characterized by) is inclusive/open‑ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims using 'comprising' as presumptively open‑ended; additional elements may be present without taking the subject matter outside the claim scope. Case examples: Mars Inc. v. H.J. Heinz; Invitrogen v. Biocrest; Genentech v. Chiron; Moleculon Research; In re Baxter; Ex parte Davis; Gillette v. Energizer (open‑ended example with razor blades). Note that context (e.g., 'group consisting of') can affect interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase: 'consisting of' (closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrase 'consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim (i.e., a closed transition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where 'consisting of' appears, there is a strong presumption the claim term is closed to unrecited elements (Multilayer Stretch Cling Film). However, the limitation applies to the clause in which it appears and may not necessarily close the entire claim if used in a subclause (Mannesmann Demag; In re Crish examples). Consider fact‑specific analysis; case law: In re Gray; Ex parte Davis; Norian v. Stryker (spatula example where added nonfunctional element did not avoid 'consisting of' limitation effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase: 'consisting essentially of' (middle ground)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Consisting essentially of' limits the claim to the specified materials or steps and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s) of the claimed invention—occupies a middle ground between 'consisting of' and 'comprising.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation depends on what the specification or claims identify as the 'basic and novel characteristics.' Absent clear intrinsic evidence, for prior art searching 'consisting essentially of' may be treated as equivalent to 'comprising.' Applicant bears burden to show additional elements/steps are excluded by demonstrating that added elements would materially change the basic/novel characteristics (In re Herz; PPG v. Guardian; AK Steel v. Sollac; In re Janakirama‑Rao; Ex parte Hoffman). If specification quantifies or describes thresholds (e.g., 'silicon should not exceed 0.5%'), that can define the permissible range under 'consisting essentially of.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Other transitional phrases (having, composed of, composed of context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'having' and 'composed of' must be interpreted in light of the specification and facts to decide whether they are open or closed; 'composed of' may be treated like 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniform open/closed meaning for terms like 'having'—interpret in view of specification and case law (Lampi; Crystal Semiconductor; Regents of Univ. of Cal. v. Eli Lilly). 'Composed of' has been interpreted either as 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on facts (AFG Industries; In re Bertsch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clauses: 'adapted to/for', 'wherein', 'whereby' (potentially limiting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clauses such as 'adapted to/for', 'wherein', and 'whereby' may raise questions as to whether they are limiting; whether they limit the claim depends on the specific facts and how they give meaning/purpose to claim steps or structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the clause imparts a structural or required functional limitation. Examples: Griffin v. Bertina (wherein clause limited a process claim by giving meaning to steps); In re Giannelli (adapted to clause limited machine claim because specification showed narrower meaning); Hoffer v. Microsoft (whereby clause material to patentability cannot be ignored). Conversely, a wherein/whereby that merely states an intended result of an already‑recited step may be given no weight (Minton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent claim limitations (method vs system claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: For method claims with contingent limitations, the broadest reasonable interpretation requires only steps that must be performed; contingent steps that depend on conditions not met are not required. For system/product claims, structure to perform a function (even if function is conditional) must be present irrespective of whether the condition occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply contingent limitation analysis differently for method and system claims. Use factual analysis of conditions precedent. PTAB decision Ex parte Schulhauser illustrates that method claims do not require performance of contingent steps when condition not met, whereas system claims require structure to perform the function if condition occurs. For obviousness rejections of system claims, prior art must teach the structure that performs the contingent function along with other recited limitations. See also MPEP § 2143.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter doctrine: determine printed matter vs functional material
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation is 'printed matter' only if it claims the content of information. If a limitation is printed matter, it is given patentable weight only if there is a new and nonobvious functional relationship between the printed matter and the physical substrate; otherwise printed matter is given no patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine if the limitation claims content of information (In re DiStefano). If so, evaluate whether the printed matter is functionally or structurally related to the substrate—if not, disregard for patentability (In re Gulack; Diamond v. Diehr). For method claims that add instructional limitations, analyze analogously whether a new and nonobvious functional relationship with the known method exists (In re DiStefano; In re Kao; King Pharm v. Eon Labs; In re Lowry; In re Ngai).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence supporting a functional relationship for printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed matter is given patentable weight when the printed matter performs some function with respect to the product (or the product performs a function with respect to the printed matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: indicia on a measuring cup that indicate volume (In re Miller); a hatband arranged so that a string of numbers satisfies a claimed algorithm (Gulack example). Look for tangible interaction where printed matter affects product operation or product arranges printed matter such that a function is performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence against a functional relationship for printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: No functional relationship exists where the product merely serves as support for printed matter or where the claim as a whole is directed to conveying a message/meaning to a human reader independent of the substrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: decorative images on a hatband not arranged in sequence; deck of playing cards with printed images; instructions in a kit that are unrelated to that specific set of chemicals (In re Gwinn; In re Bryan; In re Ngai). If printed matter and product do not depend on each other, give no patentable weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional relationship must be new and nonobvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where a functional relationship between printed matter and substrate is established, the relationship itself must be new and nonobvious for patentable weight; otherwise the claim may be anticipated or obvious over prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate novelty/nonobviousness of the claimed functional relationship. Example: color‑coded indicia indicating expiration date may be a functional relationship but still be anticipated or obvious based on prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine‑readable media claims: functional relationship test
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims are directed to a computer‑readable medium containing programming, examine the relationship between the programming and the intended computer system: if the programming performs a function with respect to the computer, a functional relationship exists and may be given patentable weight; if the medium merely supports information for human consumption, no functional relationship exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: attribute data objects that facilitate retrieval/addition/removal of information establish a functional relationship (Lowry). Memory sticks with tables of batting averages or music tracks merely support information for human readers and do not establish a functional relationship. Additionally, claims to computer‑readable media storing instructions/executable code that recite an abstract idea must be evaluated under 35 U.S.C. 101 (see MPEP § 2106).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in prior art rejections (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Express, implicit, and inherent disclosures of a prior art reference may be relied upon in rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103. Inherency is a question of fact and arises in anticipation and obviousness contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Napier; In re Grasselli. Examiner may rely on inherent teachings where a prior art embodiment necessarily possesses the claimed limitation, even if prior art did not recognize it. Use factual evidence to show inherency; inherency determinations can involve expert testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of a new property of prior art does not make it patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a previously unappreciated property or scientific explanation for a prior art composition does not render the old composition patentably new to the discoverer; claiming a new use/property that is inherently present in the prior art does not necessarily make a claim patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply cases such as Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO, In re Best, In re Crish. Even if prior art did not discuss or sequence DNA or discuss a property, if the prior art necessarily possessed the same property/sequence, it can anticipate the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by POSITA not required for inherency
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have recognized the inherent disclosure at the time of invention; the relevant inquiry is whether the subject matter is in fact inherent in the prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law: Schering v. Geneva Pharm.; Toro v. Deere; Abbott Labs v. Geneva Pharms; Atlas Powder Co. v. IRECO; SmithKline Beecham v. Apotex; In re Omeprazole. Prior art that inherently possesses claimed characteristics can be used for anticipation/obviousness even if the property was unknown or unrecognized at the time.
